overview.business_summary: Example Corp is a fictional company used to show how the app works. It makes building sensors and sells the software that office landlords use to monitor energy use, air quality and room bookings. Revenue grew 8.3% in 2024 to $1.30 billion, and about 40 cents of every sales dollar is left after the cost of making its products.

revenue_sources.name: Sensors and hardware
revenue_sources.description: Devices installed in office buildings. Customers pay once when they buy them, so sales rise and fall with new building projects.

revenue_sources.name: Software subscriptions
revenue_sources.description: Yearly fees for the dashboard that collects the sensor data. This is recurring revenue: customers keep paying as long as they keep using it.

revenue_sources.name: Installation and support
revenue_sources.description: Fees for fitting the devices and for maintenance contracts. A smaller part of sales, but it keeps customers tied to the company.

key_risks.title: Fewer new office buildings
key_risks.explanation: Hardware sales depend on construction and renovation. If landlords delay projects, sales of new sensors fall first.

key_risks.title: Reliance on a few chip suppliers
key_risks.explanation: Its sensors use chips from a small number of suppliers. A shortage would delay deliveries and raise costs.

key_risks.title: Customer data and cyber attacks
key_risks.explanation: The software stores data about buildings and the people in them. A breach could lead to fines and lost customers.

key_risks.title: Larger competitors bundling software
key_risks.explanation: Big building-management companies could include similar software for free with their own systems, which would pressure prices.

key_risks.title: Debt repayments
key_risks.explanation: The company carries $500 million of long-term debt. Higher interest rates would raise the cost of refinancing it.

management_highlights: Revenue rose 8.3% to $1.30 billion, the fifth straight year of growth, although growth has slowed each year from 11.1% in 2021.
Profit margins held steady: gross margin stayed at 40% and operating margin at 15%, so costs grew in line with sales.
Net income rose to $148 million. The 2023 figure was restated up from $130 million to $136 million.
Cash from operations of $198 million comfortably covered $60 million of equipment spending. Debt stayed at $500 million while equity grew, so debt to equity fell from 0.59 to 0.55.

agent.question: How does Example Corp make money?
agent.answer:
Example Corp makes money in three ways [10-K Item 1]:

- **Hardware**: building sensors and controllers, sold once per project. $650 million in 2024, down from $660 million.
- **Software subscriptions**: yearly fees for its Example Cloud dashboard, priced per square foot. $520 million in 2024, up 24%, now 40% of sales. This is *recurring revenue*, meaning customers keep paying each year.
- **Services**: installation, maintenance and training, $130 million.

Together that is revenue of $1.30 billion in 2024 [XBRL RevenueFromContractWithCustomerExcludingAssessedTax, FY2024]. The mix is shifting toward subscriptions, which management says drove the year's growth [10-K Item 7].

agent.question: Why did operating margin change last year?
agent.answer:
It didn't: operating margin was 15.0% in both 2023 and 2024 [computed ratio, FY2024]. *Operating margin* is the share of each sales dollar left after running costs.

Management explains that research and development ($130 million) and selling and admin costs ($195 million) grew at the same pace as revenue, and that higher-margin subscription sales offset higher chip prices in hardware, keeping gross margin at 40% [10-K Item 7]. Operating income rose to $195 million [XBRL OperatingIncomeLoss, FY2024].
